teaser: One gust of wind, two women in white, and not a single stroke of pure white paint.

lesson.text: A gust comes off the sea. In the same second, a veil flattens across a woman's face, her hand flies up to hold her hat, a skirt wraps around her knees, and a long scarf lifts from the shoulder of the younger woman walking behind. One second later, all of it will have fallen back into place.

Joaquín Sorolla painted that second on a canvas about two meters square (205 by 200 cm, close to 7 by 7 ft). The women are nearly life-size. It is an enormous picture of something that barely lasted long enough to be seen.

They are his family. The woman with the parasol is his wife, Clotilde. The one behind, bareheaded, her straw hat in her hand, is their eldest daughter, María, then nineteen. The beach is in Valencia, on Spain's Mediterranean coast, the city where Sorolla was born. The year is 1909, late in the summer, late in the afternoon.

lesson.title: What the wind does
lesson.text: Sorolla never paints the wind itself. He paints four things it is pushing.

spots.title: The veil
spots.text: A gauze veil is blown tight over Clotilde's face. You see her profile through it, tinted blue-green. Her hand rises to steady the hat.

spots.title: A stream of gauze
spots.text: The loose end of the veil flies out behind her head, so thin that the sea shows through. It is painted with a few long, dry sweeps of a wide brush.

spots.title: A handful of skirt
spots.text: Clotilde gathers her skirt in one hand, the same hand that holds the parasol's cane. The bunched cloth is thick, creamy paint, almost sculpted.

spots.title: María's scarf
spots.text: A sheer scarf balloons from María's shoulder toward her mother, closing the gap between the two figures like a sail.

lesson.text: All four of those details are white cloth. That was the challenge Sorolla set himself: two women dressed in white, under strong sun, against pale sand. A white dress painted with white paint would be a flat hole in the canvas. So what are these dresses made of?

spots.title: Violet shade
spots.text: Down María's sleeve and side, the dress is lilac and grey-blue. This is her shadow side, colored by the sky and the sea behind her.

spots.title: The closed parasol
spots.text: The folded parasol is a great pale shape tinged with pink and mauve. Only its top edge, catching the sun, comes near to pure white.

spots.title: Blue bodice
spots.text: The front of Clotilde's blouse is in shadow and painted frankly blue. Your eye still reads it as white, because it knows what a white blouse is.

spots.title: Warm hem
spots.text: Near the ground María's skirt picks up yellow and cream. The sand bounces warm light back up into the fabric.

spots.title: Shadows on sand
spots.text: The shadows cast on the beach are not brown or black. They are blue-violet, the opposite of the orange sand, which makes both colors stronger.

lesson.text: White in sunlight is never white. It borrows blue from the sky, violet from shadow and gold from the sand, and Sorolla paints the borrowing.
Sorolla liked canvases so large on the beach that the wind kept knocking them over. Photographs show his easel roped down and screens of cloth set up around him as windbreaks.

He worked fast, and had to. He said that painting outdoors slowly was impossible, because the sea, the clouds and the sun change every minute. So he loaded long brushes and covered large areas at one go. The sand at the bottom is hardly more than broad sweeps of ochre, with the weave of the canvas showing through.

The summer of 1909 was the happiest of his career. A few months earlier, an exhibition of his work in New York had drawn around 160,000 visitors in a single month. He sold close to two hundred pictures and painted the portrait of the American president, William Howard Taft. He came home rich, famous, and free to paint whatever he liked.
What he liked was this beach and these two people. There is no commission behind the picture and no story in it. He never sold it. That may explain an odd thing about the way it is framed.
Notice what is missing from the view, and what gets cut.

lines.label: No horizon, no sky
lines.text: The top edge arrives before the horizon does. Sea fills the upper part, sand the lower. You are looking down on the women from above, as if from a dune.

lines.label: A hat sliced off
lines.text: The crown of Clotilde's hat is cut by the frame. A painter composing in the studio would have left room. Sorolla crops like a snapshot.

lines.label: The walking diagonal
lines.text: From Clotilde's shoes up to María's head, the figures line up on a slant. The pair seems to be passing through the picture, on their way out of it.

lesson.text: That snapshot feeling has a source. As a teenager Sorolla earned his living retouching and coloring prints in the studio of a Valencia photographer, Antonio García. He learned there how a camera cuts into a scene. He also met the photographer's daughter. Her name was Clotilde.
When Sorolla traveled, he and Clotilde wrote to each other almost daily. Hundreds of the letters survive, many of them begging the other to hurry home.

With the crop in mind, turn to the two faces. Clotilde is hidden behind gauze and looks toward the sea. María looks down and away, her face half in shadow. Neither meets your eye. You are not invited into the walk. You are watching it go by.
Sorolla left his name and the year on the beach itself. Where?

spots.title: J. Sorolla B., 1909
spots.text: In the bottom left corner, written in dark paint on the sand. The B stands for Bastida, his mother's family name, following Spanish custom.

lesson.text: Eleven years after this walk, in 1920, Sorolla suffered a stroke while painting in the garden of his Madrid house. He never held a brush again and died in 1923. Clotilde outlived him and left the house, with everything in it, to the Spanish state.

The house is now the Museo Sorolla. The painting hangs there, in the rooms where the two women lived, a few steps from the garden. Clotilde could have sold it many times over. She kept the gust of wind at home.

quiz.question: Who are the two women?
quiz.explanation: Clotilde, his wife, walks in front; María, their daughter, follows.

quiz.question: What colors does Sorolla use for the shaded parts of the white dresses?
quiz.explanation: The shadow sides borrow blue and violet from sky and sea.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the framing?
options: The figures are tiny in a vast sky
There is no horizon and Clotilde's hat is cut off
quiz.explanation: The high viewpoint removes the sky, and the top edge slices through the hat like a snapshot.

quiz.question: What happened to Sorolla earlier in 1909?
options: He was rejected by the Madrid academy
He had a huge success with an exhibition in New York
He lost his sight in one eye
quiz.explanation: His New York show drew about 160,000 visitors in a month.

quiz.question: Where did Sorolla learn how a camera crops a scene?
options: Working in the photo studio of his future father-in-law
quiz.explanation: As a teenager he worked for the photographer Antonio García, Clotilde's father.

quiz.question: Where does the painting hang today?
options: In the family's former house in Madrid
quiz.explanation: Clotilde left the house and its contents to the state; it is now the Museo Sorolla.

facts.text: The shadows on the sand are painted blue-violet.
facts.explanation: Sorolla sets violet shadows against orange sand so that each color strengthens the other.

facts.text: Sorolla sold this painting to an American collector in 1909.
facts.explanation: He never sold it; it stayed with the family and is now in the Museo Sorolla.

facts.text: The women look straight out at the viewer.
facts.explanation: Clotilde is veiled and turned to the sea, and María looks down and away.
